#3255. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3253. Duane Betts Finally Learns to Roll With Life’s Punches

The moment Duane Betts decided to get sober, he was standing on a cliff overlooking the Pacific Ocean in California. Earlier that day, at a health food store in Malibu, where Betts was getting a smoothie and shopping with his mother, he ran into someone with whom he’d recently smoked heroin. Having not used in four days, Betts was in withdrawal. He asked the acquaintance if he was holding. The person left Betts a present in the store’s bathroom. Betts grabbed the heroin and left. Later on, while on a short hike to the ocean, with his mother waiting in the car, Betts tossed the drugs into the water. He turned around and stepped into his new life. That was 10 years ago.

“I was in sober living, and I knew they were going to test me, [so] how can I talk my way out of it when I test positive? I gave up and said, ‘I can’t do this, I’m not doing this again.’ And I never looked back,” Betts tells Rolling Stone. “It gets to the point where you’re 35 years old and you’re like, ‘Okay, I can either pull it together or I can be 60 and wonder what I could have done.’”

A decade later, the culmination of Betts’ long road to the here and now is his latest album, Isle of Hope. Produced by Dave Cobb at his Savannah, Georgia, studio, the album features 10 tracks, each co-written with Betts’ longtime collaborator, Stoll Vaughn. The project is also Betts’ debut with iconic label Sun Records. “Every record takes on a life of its own. This one came to life in the studio. It all came together very naturally and organically,” Betts says. “And Dave doesn’t mess around. He gets great sounds and he’s very instrumental in arranging the songs and bringing ideas you wouldn’t have even imagined.”

Isle of Hope is raw and real, a staggering work that is not so much about the rock, but the roll: rolling alongside the muse, rolling with the punches of life, rolling toward the unknown horizon. Sonically, it’s part rough and tumble Southern rock, part lo-fi blues, all of it heavy on melody. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“Got my shoes to shine/Looking at me and I don’t mind/Try to do my best to keep my hands clean,” Betts sings on “Keep My Hands Clean,” a song that evokes the live-wire vibe of the Rolling Stones’ Exile on Main Street.

The album title comes from the name of a bucolic unincorporated community within the Savannah metro area where Cobb’s studio is located. Filled with live oaks covered in Spanish moss and historic homes buffering the Skidaway River, Isle of Hope became a mantra of sorts for Betts each time he’d arrive.“Everyday we’d go to the studio, I kept seeing the Isle of Hope [welcome sign] and it struck me,” Betts says. “There’s a lot of crazy right now in the world and in our country, and I just thought this could be a little place where you go to get away from all that. And that’s what music is supposed to be — a little reprieve from all the noise and all the stress of the outer world.”

It’s not surprising that Betts’ musical approach comes directly from his father, the late Allman Brothers guitarist Dickey Betts. “My dad used to say, ‘When you come to an Allman Brothers Band show, we want to make you forget about the outside world for three hours,’” he recalls, “and that’s what good music does.”Growing up, Betts wanted to be a drummer and started sitting behind the kit at age five. But at 13, he switched to guitar and progressed quickly, with help from his dad. “A lot of what his playing was about was being out in nature and being at peace,” he says. “So, he would tell me to go out and play in nature when I was learning guitar.”

In 1994, when he was just 16, Betts was asked by his father to sit in with the Allman Brothers during their gig at the Gerald R. Ford Amphitheater in Vail, Colorado. “And I left my guitar at the hotel in Denver on purpose to get out of it,” Betts says with a laugh. “We were on the tour bus and my dad goes, ‘Oh, that’s okay, we have plenty.’” Related Content Allman Betts Family Revival Tour to Mark 10th Anniversary With Robert Randolph, Sierra Hull Watch Slash’s Unbelievable ‘Dreams’ Solo With Allman Betts Family Revival Devon Allman Is Carrying on the Allmans' Legacy With a New Album and Show with Slash ‘Jimmy Carter 100’ Concert Unites the B-52’s, Drive-By Truckers, India Arie in Atlanta

Something in that moment shifted within the young Betts. While playing with his father and the Allman Brothers in scenic Vail, he noted “the relief I felt and the high I felt of being part of this group of people making sound.” It was an epiphany for Betts, that he could now connect with an audience through songs.These days, Betts and his wife, Lisa, bounce between their longtime residence in Jackson, Wyoming, and Betts’ family home in Florida. In Jackson, the nature that Betts’ father was adamant his son stay in touch with is just outside the doorstep. “I kind of inherited Jackson as one of my hometowns,” Betts says. “I love the community here, and I get a lot of inspiration from the natural beauty.”

Heading into late fall and winter, Betts will hit the road with his frequent collaborator, guitarist Devon Allman, for the duo’s 10th annual holiday showcase as the Allman Betts Family Revival. Featuring guest appearances by Dweezil Zappa, Sierra Hull, Cyril Neville, Luther Dickinson, and Robert Randolph on select dates, the nationwide tour begins Nov. 28 in St. Louis and wraps up on New Year’s Eve in Tucson, Arizona. After that, Betts is set to play a slew of dates in early 2027 with his band, Palmetto Motel. Trending Stories In Praise of Andrew Scott Raye Opens Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade With 'Joy' Watch Miranda Lambert Perform Medley of Her Hits at Dallas Cowboys Halftime Show Watch 'Sesame Street' Pay Homage to Mariah Carey’s 'All I Want for Christmas Is You'

All of it, like Isle of Hope, will be carried out clear-eyed and in the moment.

“I have a vision for where I see things going. I love creating, I love to travel, and I love to play music. It’s in the fabric of who I am,” Betts says. “And I know [my dad] was really proud of me — I’m happy that he was able to see me pull it together.”

#3252. The Apple Watch Series 11 Is $100 Off in Walmart's Black Friday Sale

If you’ve been counting down to Black Friday and hoping for a deal on an Apple Watch, there’s no time like the present: Walmart recently launched its early Black Friday tech deals, and the rarely discounted Apple Watch Series 11 is currently $100 off, bringing the 42mm GPS model down to $299 (originally $399). The 46mm GPS model is $329 (originally $429), while the GPS + Cellular versions start at $399 and are also $100 off.

Though it has been supplanted by the Series 12, released earlier this fall, the Series 11 is still a great buy. It lasts up to 24 hours, making it a great option for everyday use and sleep tracking, and a 15-minute charge provides around eight hours of use. It has a strong selection of health features, including wrist temperature sensing, sleep score, ECG, heart-rate monitoring, and hypertension notifications, as well as detailed workout tracking. Compared with the Series 10, this aluminum model’s Ion-X display is twice as scratch-resistant. It’s also water-resistant to 50 meters.

While it doesn’t have the Series 12’s new processor or updated health-tracking features, the Apple Watch Series 11 is a great pick for your first Apple Watch or as an upgrade from an older model, such as the Series 8. Its large display, durability, and versatile staple features deliver the core Apple Watch experience at a more affordable price, especially if you don’t want Apple’s latest Audio Intelligence features.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3251. Walmart drops Apple Pay support from its app and website

Walmart appears to have dropped support for Apple Pay on its website and in its iPhone app. This comes just a few weeks after the retailer finally added support for Apple’s payment platform to its app and website.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

Appleosophy spotted the change last week. There’s no indication whether the feature was removed deliberately or if this is some sort of bug.

In the “Payment method” section of the checkout page on Walmart’s app and website, it no longer lists Apple Pay as an accepted payment method where it previously did. Not only that, but it doesn’t show up under the “Other ways to pay” or “More ways to pay” sections of the checkout page either.

Walmart still accepts Apple Pay in its retail stores. The retailer began rolling out contactless payment support in August, including Apple Pay, Google Pay, contactless cards, and more. For years, Walmart refused to support Apple Pay, instead trying (and failing) to convince shoppers to use its own Walmart Pay platform.

We’ll update this post if Walmart comments on Apple Pay’s disappearance from its website and app. Hopefully, it’s a bug that the company fixes sooner rather than later.

If you regularly wake up feeling stiff, notice your hips tightening after sitting for too long, or find that everyday movements leave you feeling achy, it might be time to pay attention to your mobility. While some changes in flexibility and joint movement are a natural part of aging, aches, stiffness and tension don't have to become something you put up with.

One of the best ways to keep your body moving comfortably is to make mobility work a priority. Gentle, controlled movements take your joints through their range of motion, help maintain flexibility and strengthen the muscles that support everyday movement. You don't need to spend hours stretching to see the benefits — a short routine practised regularly can be a better way to build the habit.

With that in mind, I asked Dr. Gaby Van Sickle, physical therapist and co-founder of Functional Physical Therapy, to share a 10-minute mobility workout she recommends to her clients. The routine combines simple movements to keep your hips, knees and ankles moving, build lower-body strength and support the balance and coordination we rely on as we age.

So, if you're looking for a practical way to ease stiffness and keep those everyday aches and pains at bay, here's how to fit 10 minutes of mobility into your day.

Why: Van Sickle recommends starting with walking because it’s the ideal way to prepare the body for movement. “It gradually increases blood flow to the muscles, and encourages movement through the hips, knees, ankles, and spine,” she says. “It’ll also help reduce the sensation of stiffness before beginning more targeted mobility exercises.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 4-6 per move in each direction

Why: Shoulder rolls are the ideal addition to your longevity toolkit. “They help improve mobility through the shoulders and upper back, which makes movements like reaching overhead and getting dressed easier,” Van Sickle says. Over time, they’ll help ease aching in the shoulders and neck.

Why: Neck and lower back stiffness are common, and it’s usually caused by too much pressure or tension in this area. “Thoracic rotations help relieve this by distributing movement throughout the trunk,” Van Sickle explains.

Time: 1 minute Reps: 8-10 of each movement per leg

Why: Van Sickle recommends these moves frequently to her clients because they promote active hip mobility while strengthening the gluteal muscles. Keeping the hips mobile and the surrounding muscles strong can help reduce feelings of stiffness and make everyday movements, like walking and stepping to the side, feel more comfortable.

Why: “This is a functional movement that promotes mobility and strength through the core, hips, knees, and ankles,” Van Sickle says. Staying active in these areas helps reduce stiffness in the lower body.

Why: Stiff ankles and tight lower-leg muscles can make walking feel less comfortable. Practicing calf raises and toe raises moves the ankle in both directions while strengthening the muscles around it, which will help support a smoother, more comfortable stride.

Time: 1 minute Reps: 15-30 marches per leg

Why: Standing marches gently move the hips and knees while encouraging you to shift your weight from one leg to the other. “It’s about keeping the lower body moving to ease feelings of stiffness after periods of sitting or inactivity,” Van Sickle advocates.

If aches, stiffness and tension are making everyday movement feel more difficult, a regular mobility routine can help. These exercises gently move your hips, knees and ankles through their range of motion while strengthening the muscles that support your joints, helping you maintain the mobility, balance and strength you need as you age.

The key is consistency, rather than pushing yourself to do more. Try setting aside 10 minutes each day to work through the routine, moving slowly and staying within a comfortable range of motion. Over time, a regular practice can help you feel less stiff after periods of inactivity and more confident with everyday movements.

#3247. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

#3246. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

Update 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3240. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. Three sessions were held in the United States and one session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled later this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos, past chair of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Soudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

You don't have to write a single line of code to appreciate what it can do

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Claude Code might sound like something exclusively reserved for software engineers, but you don't need to know a single programming language to put Anthropic's AI agent to work.

While Claude is great for answering questions, brainstorming ideas and writing emails, Claude Code can work directly with files on your computer, execute commands and tackle projects that would otherwise require several different apps.

The beauty of Claude Code is that you can describe what you want done in plain English and let the AI handle the technical side. From tackling an embarrassingly messy Downloads folder to making sense of years of family photos, here are seven surprisingly practical ways to use Claude Code that have nothing to do with programming, along with the prompts to get started.

If your Downloads folder has become a digital junk drawer filled with screenshots, PDFs, receipts and files you don't even remember downloading, Claude Code can help you sort through the mess.

Rather than manually opening every file and figuring out where it belongs, you can ask Claude to categorize documents, suggest more descriptive file names and organize copies into subfolders.

What makes this particularly useful is that Claude Code can do the actual organizational work rather than simply recommend a folder structure for you to create yourself.

Prompt: Review the files in this folder and organize them into meaningful categories based on their contents. Identify potential duplicates and suggest descriptive file names. Show me your proposed organization before making any changes. Do not delete or overwrite anything.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Most banking apps tell you how much you've spent, but they don't necessarily give you the level of detail you want about your spending habits.

Download a CSV of your transactions, remove sensitive personal and account information and give Claude Code a copy. You can ask it to categorize expenses, identify recurring subscriptions and create a customized spreadsheet with charts that visualize your spending.

You could even have Claude identify subscriptions that have gone up in price or calculate how much you're spending on takeout compared to groceries.

Instead of paying for another budgeting app, you can create a financial dashboard tailored to the information you actually care about.

Prompt: Analyze this CSV of my transactions. Categorize my spending, identify recurring subscriptions, flag unusual expenses and create an Excel dashboard with monthly spending trends and potential savings. Do not modify the original file or invent missing information.

Between screenshots, phone backups and photos transferred from old devices, it's surprisingly easy to accumulate thousands of poorly organized images.

Claude Code can use available image metadata to sort photos by date, identify exact duplicates and create a more manageable folder structure without requiring you to drag and drop hundreds of files.

You can also ask it to separate screenshots from camera photos where possible, making it easier to find the pictures you actually want to keep.

I'd recommend starting with a small batch of copied photos before tackling your entire collection.

Prompt: Review the photos in this folder and use available metadata to organize copies by year and month. Identify exact duplicates and screenshots. Flag photos with missing dates rather than guessing. Preserve every original image and create a summary of what you've organized.

As a mom of three, I know how quickly school newsletters, sports schedules, permission slips and appointment reminders can pile up. Keeping track of everything often means digging through multiple emails and attachments just to figure out what's happening next week.

Save those documents in a dedicated folder and ask Claude Code to extract important dates, deadlines, locations and reminders.

The AI can generate an .ics calendar file that you can review and import into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook. That saves you from having to manually create an event for every soccer practice, school concert or early dismissal.

Prompt: Review all the documents in this folder and extract important dates, deadlines, appointments and events. Create a chronological schedule and an importable .ics calendar file. Include locations and relevant notes. Flag conflicting or ambiguous dates for my review rather than making assumptions.

Before you spend money on additional cloud storage or an external hard drive, it might be worth finding out what's actually eating up space on your computer.

Claude Code can examine selected folders, identify unusually large files, locate exact duplicates and generate a report showing where you could potentially reclaim storage.

You could discover everything from forgotten video exports to multiple copies of the same large presentation. You can also ask Claude to break down its findings in plain English so you know what you're looking at before deciding what to remove.

The key here is to have Claude investigate rather than automatically delete anything.

Prompt: Perform a read-only storage audit of this folder. Identify the largest files, exact duplicates, old downloads and unusually large subfolders. Create a report showing potential storage savings and explain which files I should review manually. Do not delete, move or modify anything.

If your favorite recipes are scattered across screenshots, Word documents, PDFs and random text files, Claude Code can help you turn them into something you might actually use.

Give Claude a folder containing your recipes and ask it to extract the ingredients, standardize the formatting and categorize everything into a collection. You can even have it produce a printable PDF cookbook with a cover and table of contents.

For something more personal, you could turn a collection of family recipes into a homemade cookbook to give relatives for the holidays.

Prompt: Turn the recipes in this folder into a professionally formatted PDF cookbook. Organize them by meal type, create a table of contents and standardize ingredient lists and instructions. Preserve the original measurements and flag any missing information instead of inventing it.

Creating a home inventory is one of those things most of us know we should do but never quite get around to.

Having an organized record of your belongings, receipts and warranties could make life considerably easier when you need to file an insurance claim, replace an appliance or find out whether something is still under warranty.

Claude Code can work through a collection of receipts, product manuals and photos to create a home inventory spreadsheet. It can also organize copies of supporting documents so they're easier to find when you need them.

You could even ask Claude to create a separate maintenance schedule for household appliances based on their instruction manuals.

Prompt: Review the receipts, manuals and product photos in this folder. Create a home inventory spreadsheet with product names, model numbers, purchase dates, prices, warranty information and links to supporting files. Mark anything you cannot verify as unknown. Preserve all original documents.

What makes Claude Code interesting beyond programming is its ability to bridge the gap between getting advice from an AI chatbot and actually getting something done.

Of course, giving an AI agent access to your computer comes with risks. I recommend starting with a dedicated folder containing copies of your documents, reviewing permission requests carefully and keeping backups of anything important. Always double-check the finished results, particularly when dealing with financial information or important deadlines.

#3235. An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it …

I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the company did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

So if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The company solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.

Prime Video is wrapping up 2026 with another month of movies and TV shows to add to your watchlist. December brings a fresh batch of streaming releases, whether you’re looking for a new series to binge, a festive movie to get you into the holiday spirit or something exciting to watch over the Christmas break.

As always, I’ll be keeping this guide updated throughout December with everything arriving on Prime Video, including release dates and new episodes of ongoing shows. So, if you’re wondering what to watch next, here’s everything new coming to Prime Video this month.

Prime Video is getting into the festive spirit with “The Man with the Bag,” a Christmas action-comedy that brings together Arnold Schwarzenegger and “Reacher” star Alan Ritchson. I think this looks like a really fun pairing, especially with the film leaning into a passing-of-the-torch moment between two generations of action heroes. It’s also Schwarzenegger’s first feature film appearance since 2019's “Terminator: Dark Fate,” and his first Christmas movie in 30 years, following “Jingle All the Way.” Ritchson, meanwhile, brings plenty of action-star appeal of his own and also serves as a producer.

When Santa Claus (Arnold Schwarzenegger) discovers that his iconic red bag of presents has been stolen by a rogue elf named Nadia (Awkwafina), Christmas is suddenly in jeopardy. With his busiest night of the year fast approaching, Santa turns to Vance (Alan Ritchson), a skilled thief who has found himself on the Naughty List. Tasked with recovering the missing bag, Vance puts together a crew of criminally talented misfits to help pull off an ambitious heist. With assistance from Santa, his elves and a few reindeer, the unlikely team must work together to retrieve the stolen sack before Christmas arrives.

Stream "The Man with the Bag" on Prime Video from Dec. 2

“Sacred Jewel” is shaping up to be one of Prime Video’s biggest international drama releases of the year. This South Korean historical action-romance series reunites director Jung Dae-yoon with veteran actor Lee Sung-min, following their hugely successful 2022 drama “Reborn Rich.” That series became one of the highest-rated Korean cable dramas in television history, so there’s already plenty of anticipation surrounding their latest collaboration. The story brings together wartime action and elements of spiritual folklore, offering a little something for fans of historical dramas and adventure.

Set in 1258 during the Goryeo Dynasty, “Sacred Jewel” follows a kingdom on the brink of defeat after nearly three decades of war against the Mongol Empire. With its future hanging in the balance, young warrior Baek Gyul (Ahn Bo-hyun) is appointed to lead an elite expedition tasked with recovering the Avalokitesvara Jewel, a sacred relic believed to possess the power to protect the kingdom. Joined by experienced soldiers and a resourceful guide, the group sets out across enemy territory towards the eastern sea. Meanwhile, Princess Wang Hee (Claudia Kim) ventures beyond the safety of the palace to help the expedition.

“Maxton Hall: The World Between Us” is returning for its third and final season, bringing Prime Video’s hugely popular German romantic drama to a close. The six-episode conclusion follows the structure of Mona Kasten’s bestselling book trilogy, with each season adapting one of the novels: “Save Me,” “Save You” and “Save Us.” Despite being set at an elite British boarding school and in Oxford, the series uses historic German landmarks to bring its lavish world to life. It’s been one of Prime Video’s biggest international hits, so fans have plenty of reason to look forward to this final chapter.

The third season picks up after Ruby Bell’s (Harriet Herbig-Matten) suspension from Maxton Hall College. With her dream of studying at Oxford hanging in the balance, Ruby is determined to clear her name, despite evidence suggesting that her boyfriend, James Beaufort (Damian Hardung), is responsible for her expulsion. The pair join forces to uncover the truth and save Ruby’s graduation, but their search brings unexpected revelations that threaten to change everything. Meanwhile, James’ friends and those closest to the couple find themselves caught up in the fallout.

#3231. Microsoft declares a Code Red in response to worst ever outage

The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour …

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

“Scattered across fragmented internal systems.” 😆

As someone who works in IT and manages Microsoft products, I thought that was their entire design philosophy.

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.
