#3155. Channel 4 Defends Huw Edwards Doc After Government Criticism: “There Is Clear Public Interest In Confronting Him With Questions”

Channel 4 has been forced to defend its Huw Edwards doc three days before it premieres, with the network’s news chief saying the film has “clear public interest.”

Channel 4 unveiled Huw Edwards – Guilty last week and it will air Tuesday night. It has already been met with a barrage of criticism including from the upper echelons of UK government.

News chief Louisa Compton issued a rare and lengthy statement this morning, saying: “We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film. But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest.” Related Stories News BBC Being Investigated Over Antisemitism By Government Adviser News Huw Edwards To Speak On TV For First Time About Criminal Actions & Fall From Grace In Channel 4 Doc

The statement came after the Prime Minister’s spokesperson said the country has “no interest in hearing what [Edwards] has to say,” while paying tribute to the “victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation.” Watch on Deadline

Compton joined with government in saying that behind Edwards’ offences are “real children and real victims – including those as young as seven – who have been abused.”

But she stressed that the disgraced ex-BBC News anchor “is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms,” and was not paid or given editorial control.

“Journalism isn’t about only putting people on television whose actions or opinions we approve of,” she added. “Sometimes its purpose is precisely the opposite: to look directly at people who have done terrible things, confront them with difficult questions, test their explanations and allow audiences to judge what they say for themselves.”

Compton, who was recently promoted to Director of News, Digital and Audience Trust, said the doc “raises wider and uncomfortable questions about power, trust and accountability, and about how our criminal justice system responds to people convicted of offences involving indecent images of children.”

Airing on Tuesday night, the doc will be the first time Edwards has spoken publicly on TV about his conviction and fall from grace. He has addressed his actions on his Substack but this will be the first time he speaks about them with an interviewer. A short trailer sees Edwards say “I’d lost the plot” after being questioned over why he did what he did. The interviewer can then be heard saying exasperatedly, “Oh, come on.”

Allegations of grooming and paying younger people for sexually explicit images were published about Edwards in 2023 by The Sun and the following year he pled guilty to making indecent images of children. He has since mostly retreated from public life, returning to where he grew up in Wales, which is where the doc takes place.

“It is reasonable to ask why Channel 4 has made this film, and why now. As a public service broadcaster, we have a responsibility to think very carefully about what we put on screen, balancing the public interest in asking difficult questions of powerful people against the potential impact on our audiences, and particularly on victims and survivors of abuse.

We did not take that decision lightly. Journalism isn’t about only putting people on television whose actions or opinions we approve of. Sometimes its purpose is precisely the opposite: to look directly at people who have done terrible things, confront them with difficult questions, test their explanations and allow audiences to judge what they say for themselves. The circumstances and gravity are of course very different, but journalists routinely interview and hold to account people who have committed dreadful acts, including murderers, terrorists and dictators. The principle is the same: interviewing someone is not an endorsement of them. It is an opportunity to challenge what they have done, interrogate their account and allow audiences to judge their answers for themselves.

That is what this film does. Huw Edwards is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms. He is questioned throughout by an experienced director; he was not paid; he had no control over the content of the film; and there were no restrictions on the questions he could be asked.

Edwards was one of the most prominent and trusted broadcasters in Britain. He pleaded guilty to serious offences involving indecent images of children and has never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation. There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered.

We are also acutely conscious that behind offences involving indecent images are real children and real victims – including those as young as seven – who have been abused. Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards’ participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation. His account is there to be tested, not accepted.

Channel 4’s remit is also to stimulate debate. This film raises wider and uncomfortable questions about power, trust and accountability, and about how our criminal justice system responds to people convicted of offences involving indecent images of children. Those questions extend far beyond one disgraced public figure and deserve serious scrutiny.

Channel 4 has a long and established record of investigating powerful figures and confronting serious wrongdoing. That same journalistic instinct applies here: holding people to account sometimes means investigating them from the outside, and sometimes it means gaining access, challenging them directly and testing the account they give of their actions.

We should be capable of examining difficult issues rather than looking away because we don’t like what we see. We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film. But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest.”

#3154. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3153. These Are the Best Last Minute Black Friday Tool Deals at Home Depot

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have some big home projects to tackle this winter or if you’re looking for a gift for a DIY enthusiast in your life, you might be looking for some new tools. Black Friday sales are often the lowest prices of the year on quality tools, so now is a good time to look for extra savings at Home Depot.

Getting a cordless combo set if you’re starting a new tool kit is a good way to save money and set yourself up with batteries and chargers for your new tools. Here are some deals on quality cordless tool sets that will keep working for years.

The Milwaukee 9-tool 18-volt combo kit is on sale for $699 at Home Depot, 50% off its regular price. This set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a work light, an impact wrench, a Sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, an angle grinder, a circular saw, a blower, two 4-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and two tool bags. This is a good-quality starter set that has all the tools you need for simple maintenance and repair projects as well as projects like putting up shelves, fixing a fence, or installing a sink.

The Milwaukee 5-tool, 18-volt combo set is on sale at Home Depot for $349, 50% off its usual price. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, an oscillating multi-tool, a Sawzall, a work light, a 4-amp-hour battery, a 2-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a simple tool set that allows you to tackle basic repairs like a drywall patch and also some maintenance tasks like changing air filters.

The Milwaukee 4-tool 18-volt Packout set is on sale for $699, 42% off its typical price. This set also qualifies for a free battery with purchase deal that gets you a free 18-volt, 8-amp-hour battery. Just click the “free gift” button on the menu to the right and select the battery to get the deal. The new price will show up in your cart. The set comes with a hammer drill, an impact driver, an angle grinder, a sawzall, a rolling tool case, two 5-amp-hour batteries, and a charger. If you plan to transport your tools, the Packout system is a convenient way to keep your tools organized.

Hand tools and bits are a big part of a well-appointed home tool set, and a part that is often overlooked until a third or fourth trip to the hardware store. Saving some money on these tools will also save you time and aggravation while you’re working on your DIY projects.

The Shockwave 15-piece impact-duty drill bit set is on sale for $19.97, 43% off its regular price. This set comes with 15 impact-compatible titanium SAE drill bits ranging from 1/16-inches to ⅜-inches. This is a good set for any projects that involve drilling through multiple materials, like installing a bracket for a flat screen in a wall stud.

A two-pack of Milwaukee utility knives with a fold-out screwdriver is on sale for $19.97, 55% off its usual price. These knives have blades that are simple to change out, and they’re a perfect stocking stuffer for anyone who works with their hands.

A two-pack of Milwaukee 25-foot magnetic tape measures is on sale for $19.97, 57% off its typical price. You can never have enough tape measures if you do any kind of woodworking or construction, and these make a great gift for anyone who likes to DIY.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools.

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3152. X finally gets six parental controls for teen accounts, but kids must consent

Most social media platforms have long had parental controls to give oversight into the ways teens are using the service and to ensure they get appropriate content in their feeds. X has finally joined the party.

#3150. Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Kicks Off, Making History On A Dry And Breezy Saturday

With New York City temperatures in the mid-40s with some light breezes and no rain, the postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade got underway this morning at 8:30 a.m. ET, making history as the first such parade to make its way through Manhattan in the event’s 100 year history.

Two of this year’s hosts, NBC’s Savannah Guthrie and Hoda Kotb, welcomed viewers, calling the event historic and unprecedented. Guthrie said, “To the city, to the volunteers, to the crews and performers and the more than 11,000 people who made this parade happen and insisted upon it, thank you. You made sure that not only would the show go on but that it would be every bit as spectacular as the 100th deserves.” Related Stories News Broadway Gets Speed-Dating-Style Tribute At Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade News The Show Must Go On: Broadway Will Perform Saturday In Macy's Thanksgiving Parade

“Every balloon, float, every surprise,” Guthrie continued, “is still on, and because it is the parade is the 100th some iconic inflatables are coming out of the archives for the first time in decades.” (One of those classics is the ’60s cartoon character Underdog.) Watch on Deadline

British singer-songwriter Raye along with her sisters Amma and Absolutely got things off to a musical start, performing just before the parade itself stepped off. Paddington the Bear – apparently the costumed performer/remote-control puppet hybrid that appears in the upcoming Paddington Broadway musical – made an early appearance, chatting with Guthrie and Kodb in the interview area (the bear will return later atop its own parade float.)

Postponed from Thursday due to severe weather – torrential rains, high winds – that would have endangered participants and spectators (and certainly would have grounded the giant floating balloons that are a cherished element of the event) the parade is expected to include nearly all of the performers, marching bands and Broadway shows that were initially planned.

The parade will be broadcast on NBC and will stream on Peacock.

There were some last-minute changes: At least two marching bands, including The Macy’s Great American Marching Band, the annual ensemble of high school musicians from across the country, and University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band, which returned home to perform at the annual Alabama-Auburn matchup known as the Iron Bowl.

And while Macy’s has not at this writing released an official parade line-up, organizers previously noted that 95% of the line-up initially scheduled for Thursday would be on hand today, with two newcomers – LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor – added to the linup. That original lineup included Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, JoJo and Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, as well as a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete. Newly added Gaynor is expected to sing her signature song “I Will Survive.”

According to Macy’s last year’s parade – the broadcast of which was rerun on Thursday – drew about 3.5 million in-person spectators, and a similar number is expected today.

What Macy’s is calling the “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will go on as planned, with performers from The Lost Boys, The Rocky Horror Show, Wicked, Schmigadoon!, Aladdin, The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Hamiilton and the 30th-anniversary tribute to Rent taking part in the first-of-its-kind, 14-minute Broadway medley (traditionally, the participating Broadway shows perform on their own, one at a time.)

Paddington the Musical is confirmed to participate in the Saturday broadcast as a separate float, as originally intended.

As for those high school and college marching bands that each year travel from around the country to participate in the parade, this year’s participants had to scramble to make the travel and hotel accommodations – and raise the necessary funding – necessitated by the delay. And nearly all seem to have done so successfully: The last few days saw the schools’ local communities and sponsors step up to help cover the costs, and just today Macy’s announced that it is donating $50,000 to the music program of every school band in the parade to defray this year’s costs. (Various bands have been posting on social media about their efforts to raise the tens and even hundreds of thousands of dollars needed for an additional couple days in New York City.)

As for that delay, while Thursday’s weather began reasonably mild – prompting some keyboard critics to question the decision to delay, and some MAGA types criticizing New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for pulling the plug – the feared storm most certainly did arrive by late morning Thursday, and continued to intensify through the day, causing flooding, downed trees and electrical outages throughout the New York City area.

Macy’s has been especially careful with the giant balloons after a 1998 incident in which an inflatable Cat in the Hat was blown off course by gusts and smashed into a lamppost, sending a large piece of metal tumbling into the crowd of spectators, injuring four people, including a woman who spent nearly a month in a coma.

A two-pack of DeWalt 20-volt MAX 2-amp-hour batteries is on sale at Home Depot for $79, 53% off its regular price.

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds comes with a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation. They're $149 on Amazon (originally $249) as an early Black Friday deal.

The Bose QuietComfort 2nd Gen is currently down to $199 (originally $359), its lowest price ever. The Bose QuietComfort line has been around for a long time, excelling in comfort, ANC, and minimalism. As PCMag mentions in their review, their sound profile leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 came out in 2025 and are the best over-ear headphones I tested last year (or ever, really). These headphones go with a companion app that's packed with a lot more features that you can nerd out on. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever.

Samsung’s 32-inch Odyssey G5 (G51F) gaming monitor has dropped to $179.99 on Amazon, which is the lowest price it has reached so far. It’s a flat panel (unlike Samsung’s many curved gaming displays), with a matte coating that helps minimize glare in brighter rooms, and comes with a stand that supports height, tilt, and pivot adjustments. The G51F’s combination of 180Hz refresh rate, 1ms response time, and AMD FreeSync support makes fast-paced games look smoother and feel more responsive than they do on standard 60Hz displays, especially in shooters, racing games, and competitive multiplayer titles.

If you're interested in the new M5 MacBook, Amazon is the only major retailer offering a $250 discount. The 15-inch MacBook Air is $1,199.99 (originally $1,499), and the new M5 chip is powerful enough to likely carry all of your workload without hiccups. Other sizes and configurations are also up to $300 off.

Budget TVs have improved dramatically over the years, and the Hisense U6 Series is a great example of what you can get today for a "budget" price. This is a QLED Mini LED TV, so while it's not at the quality that OLED TVs can offer, it makes up for it with a much lower price. Right now, the 65-inch Hisense Class U6 Series TV is $529.99 (originally $1,099.99), the lowest price it has been. Don't let the budget price fool you; this is a quality TV. The best one of 2025, according to PCMag's "outstanding" review. Its main attributes are its incredible levels of brightness, peaking at 1,024 nits, and its beautiful colors. This is expected from a QLED Mini LED TV, but not for under $550 for a 65-inch TV. It is also packed with features and specs that you won't find in other TVs at this price.

Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $997.99 (originally $2,499.99), its lowest price since it launched in April. The QM8L has a “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits; no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming, and contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

The Hisense E7SF QLED is in the low to mid-range of the OLED category, but with its 45% discount, the price is much lower. Amazon currently has the 65-inch E7SF QLED for $499.99 (originally $999.99), which is especially notable given this model came out in April of this year. The first thing you'll notice about the Hisense E7 is how thin and lightweight it is. It comes with four HDMI connections, one of which is an eARC connection so you can plug in a soundbar, and two with a native 144Hz refresh rate in game mode.

A sketchy rumor is doing the rounds suggesting that Apple is working on a ceramic edition of the iPhone 20 Pro.

Ceramic? For a phone? C’mon. Sketchy is an understatement.

There are no details, and while one concept image shows a ceramic back, this seems a rather unlikely possibility …

Fixed Focus Digital is one of those pointing to the possibility, stating that they have seen ceramic components for next year’s flagship iPhone. An image has also been shared by Tech Overwatch, which is very clearly a render, simply imagining what it might look like.

#3142. Broadway Gets Speed-Dating-Style Tribute At Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade’s “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” went off without a hitch, even if it seemed more like a Broadway-themed speed-dating exercise. Nine musical productions – a mix of long-running shows and newcomers – were each given about a minute to show their stuff and pitch a nationwide audience on buying a ticket or two and taking in a Broadway show.

Broadway’s big parade moment arrived at 9:13 a.m. ET, nearly 45 minutes into the event, with emcee Julianne Hough (soon to hit Broadway in Damn Yankees) arriving with some formally clad backup dancers to stake a perch on a couch to watch the medley. Related Stories News Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Kicks Off, Making History On A Dry And Breezy Saturday News The Show Must Go On: Broadway Will Perform Saturday In Macy's Thanksgiving Parade

The medley began with Lissa deGuzman and the Chicago ensemble performing an energetic “All That Jazz,” and then, a minute later, Tony nominees Sara Chase and Alex Brightman of Schmigadoon! taking over the performance space to sing that show’s opening title number (with Brightman’s spoken “I hate musicals!” joke intact.) Watch on Deadline

Next, at 9:15, came Hamilton, represented her by cast member Jarrod Spector, in full regal cape and crown as King George II and singing that musical’s comic showstopper “You’ll Be Back.” Another crowd-pleaser followed (at 9:16) when Margaret Cho (in character as the narrator of The Rocky Horror Show) led her cast mates in a rousing minute of “Let’s Do The Time Warp.”

Next up were some original members of the cast of Rent, performing “Seasons of Love,” followed by LJ Benet and Maria Wirries of The Lost Boys, perched high above the street on a tower of scaffolding, performing “Now, Forever.”

At 9:19 Sherri Shepherd, in full Genie regalia, was joined by Rodney Ingram as the title character from Disney’s Aladdin to sing that musical’s “Friend Like Me,” then it was quickly on to The Book of Mormon, with the dancing and singing Mormons performing the show’s signature tune “Tomorrow Is a Latter Day.”

The final bit of the medley went to Wicked, with the current Broadway Elphaba (Keri René Fuller) and Glinda (Emma Flynn), performing the big number “Defying Gravity,” complete with the Wicked Witch’s very, very large, billowing black cape that would never have survived the gusts of Thanksgiving Thursday.

The medley, created and choreographed by Sarah O’Gleby with composer Tom Kitt arranging the music, was a solid and affectionate attempt at honoring Broadway, though many fans and industry insiders will likely be left with a little holiday nostalgia for the days when each show got its own spotlight to perform a full musical number, like the thrilling Ragtime number last year (or last Thursday, as it turned out with the rerun) or the boundary-pushing performance from The Prom in 2018 when NBC’s cameras zoomed in on a sweet little high school prom kiss that, like today’s Saturday parade, made a bit of history itself: Emma Nolan and Alyssa Greene, the Prom‘s ingenue stars, delivered the first same-sex kiss in parade history, to the delighted cheers and applause of the gathered spectators.

#3140. MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air: Which should you buy right now?

Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo

Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

There are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is currently on sale with a starting price of $999.

For that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

The MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

As I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

The M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

One of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

To recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

Beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

What do you think of the MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air decision? Which would you choose? Let us know down in the comments.

There are few things greater in life than a full surround system with a projector — just like you'll find at the movie theater. There are just a few problems with getting that experience at home — chiefly, price. Even less elaborate home theater systems can cost thousands of dollars, and that's not something all of us have to hand. I know I don't. I have a car to pay for.

Then there's the space it takes up, and wiring you have to do. Surround systems take up loads of room, with speakers permanently placed around the room. That means wiring in the walls (or, if you're lazy, across the floor) and expensive mounting on walls. Not ideal.

But it needn't be any of these things. You can make an excellent home cinema system for around $1,000 thanks to pretty special Black Friday deals. So I set myself a challenge — get everything you'd need for a home cinema system, including accessories, for that key G of a price point. I'm $3 out. Let's see how I did.

A wireless soundbarJBL Bar 800Arguably as important (if not more so) than the display you've got going, the audio system acts as the core of your home theater setup. But we want ours to be wireless — so this, the JBL Bar 800, is perfect. It not only features a wireless subwoofer, but also a pair of wireless surrounds that don't even need to be plugged into the wall for power. Just take them off the sides of the soundbar when you want to watch a movie, then place them in the optimum surround position. The soundbar does the rest — it listens to itself and then adjusts its sound profile. Now we're off to the races — wireless Dolby Atmos Top Gun: Maverick, here we come, baby.

The projectorSoundcore Nebula P1iThis is the picture bit — without it you're not going to have any idea about what's going on in your favorite movies. This is just a 1080p option, so you're not going to want to blow the image up too big — things will quickly start to look pixelated and, like, bad — but sit at a suitable distance away and you can easily get away with a 90-inch screen. There are two reasons I've gone for this option. The first is that it's got Google TV built in, so you don't need any extra hardware to stream all those movies. The second is that it's portable, which means you can fold it up and pack it away when you're done.

A stand for your projectorNebula Quick-Mount Projector StandOne of the most important parts of a projector setup is how you mount it. Now, we're looking to put ours away when we're done, so you can really mount it on the wall. This projector stand matches our projector, and it's compact enough that we can put it away with the projector. You can also adjust the height more easily, so that you can place the projector behind a sofa or something. Underrated home theater feature: the mounting. Get it wrong, and you're not watching anything.

The screen120inch Projector Screen with StandYou could just point your projector at a wall and hope for the best — but unless it's perfectly flat and white you're in for a less-than-optimal time. This massive screen unfolds and sits upright, ready to receive a massive image. When you're done, it folds back down, ready for next time. Mission accomplished, baybee.

Look, I know. I've done the math. I'm $3 over budget. But $3 is $3, and that's more than the budget. Just sell your socks or something.

Oh, I nailed this one. The subwoofer and surrounds don't need to plug into the soundbar; they communicate wirelessly. The only wire you'll need to worry about connects the soundbar to the projector. Not totally wireless then, but there would be ways of going totally wireless, like this wireless HDMI adapter (which is now just $60 instead of $199 at Amazon this Black Friday).

Everything here can be packed away when you're done. The surround speakers click back into the soundbar, and the projector and screen can be folded into smaller packages and put away when you're done. No-one will ever know they were there.

No, it's not 4K — but that would jack the price up by far too much. These components are all great quality pieces of kit. If there's one that you buy from the list, though, make sure it's the soundbar — it sounds great, and the surround speakers are a very cool addition.

#3136. ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Warming Up $83M+ 5-Day As Thanksgiving Stretch Box Office Sees $220M+ – Update

SATURDAY AM: The Thanksgiving five-day stretch for all movies is coming in at an estimated at $220M+ per sources, which isn’t the worst we’ve seen post Covid; higher than 2021, 2022 and 2023, but certainly far off as we always expected from 2024’s all-time high of $424.9M (-48%) and even last year’s fifth best ever ($290.3M, -24%).

Thank God for Lionsgate, Suzanne Collins and Francis Lawrence for resuscitating The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which is now seeing a Wednesday-Sunday estimate of $83.5M, because Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed (with a $33M-$34M 5-day) isn’t cutting it, and Universal/Paramount’s Ariana Grande-Ben Stiller-Robert De Niro Focker In-Law (coming in with $40.1M) is more counter programming than an event (which is still essential in the diversity of a box office marketplace).

But any easing we’re seeing at the Thanksgiving box office will be made up greatly by the end of the year as Disney/Marvel Studio’s Avengers: Doomsday and Warner Bros/Legendary’s Dune: Part III shoot for the best weekend ever at the North American B.O., potentially surpassing this year’s July 31-Aug 3 frame of $437.1M. Watch on Deadline

Focker In-Law in regards to domestic box office to budget, $40.1M opening to $90M production cost, should be fine before we start counting International which Paramount is handling. It’s slightly cheaper than the $100M of 2010’s Little Fockers, yet more expensive than 2004’s Meet the Fockers $80M (unadjusted for inflation). Among the openings in the Meet the Parents franchise, Focker In-Law is third behind Meet the Fockers (amazing Christmas 5-day of $70.5M, $46.1M 3-day; that would be sweet to achieve those numbers on a pure comedy nowadays) and Little Fockers‘ $45M 5-day during Christmas 2010.

Word of mouth on this movie was mixed according to RelishMix who weighed it at a 5.2 out of 10 on their buzz meter. While there’s a contingency that appreciate the gender flip of Ariana Grande in lead versus the franchise being a mere retread, there’s others on social who yell “enough already” and that the franchise is akin to “beating a dead horse.” Grande, though clearly the draw here, is a double-edged sword according to what RelishMix is spotting with some believing that they’re watching her as opposed to the multi hyphenate playing another character in the film.

Hexed is another Thanksgiving bomb for Walt Disney Animation following 2023’s Wish ($31.6M 5-day) and 2022’s Strange World ($18.8M). To think that 11 years ago, Disney got dragged over the underperformance of Pixar’s Good Dinosaur ($55.5M 5-day, $123M final domestic, $332M WW, $175M-$200M production cost), but at that box office threshold, that movie was a hit by today’s results. Hexed, despite audiences enjoying it at an A-, is a tad out of season with its story of a mother-and-daughter witch, having a more Halloween vibe than say Wicked (which is squarely rooted in the Wizard of Oz). Not to mention, there’s no original songs to take this property to another atmopsheric level, rather non-fresh needle drops, i.e. Dua Lipa’s six-year-old “Levitating” and The Car’s 42-year old song “Magic.” Hailee Steinfeld can sing beautifully — why isn’t she singing throughout this entire movie? The industry can cry about how hard it is to launch original animated films, that streaming is butting in on the subgenre, however, history has shown that it’s possible to make a sublime, largely unique tale with compelling characters and emotional songs, i.e. Disney’s Frozen and Pixar’s Coco.

RelishMix saw the lackluster word-of-mouth on social ahead of opening with “Mixed-negative leaning chatter for Hexed with the dominant complaint being structural vibes as viewers accuse the film of lifting The Owl House’s series skeleton while surgically removing its queerness. There’s a sharp sub-thread lamenting, ‘gender-swap of the lead from boy to girl.’ Comments accuse ‘the studio designed every shot for TikTok rather than the big screen’ while others compare the shift to a franchise precedent: ‘When I heard they changed the gender of the protagonist, all I could think of is how they destroyed Chicken Little by forcing a male protagonist years into the movie’s development.'”

The social media universe reach for Hexed across TikTok, YouTube, X, Instagram and Facebook was OK, though not spectacular, with 400 million followers, which which is slightly higher than Universal/DreamWorks Animation’s original title Forgotten Island (382.8M followers), higher than Elemental (301M followers) and Wish (343.6M).

A history of the Thanksgiving domestic marketplace:

FRIDAY AM: Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping saw the second best Thanksgiving and Thursday of the franchise with $11.6M after Catching Fire‘s $14.95M 13 years ago and ahead of Mockingjay Part 2‘s $11M in 2014.

The running cume of the sixth feature adaptation of the Suzanne Collins series is $174.9M with an $85M 5-day still within reach. Yesterday, the fifth Francis Lawrence directed Hunger Games pic flew past the $166.3M lifetime cume its predecessor, 2023’s Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes‘ $166.3M. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s running total by Sunday looks stand around $233M, which will be 17% ahead of Mockingjay 2 at the same point in time and +3% ahead of Mockingjay 1. Both titles respectively ended their domestic runs at $282M and $337.1M. The highest grossing Hunger Games title is Catching Fire with $425.3M.

All pics at the Thanksgiving Box Office rang up an estimated $35.6M, -9% from last year’s Thanksgiving. Business is expected to go up to $59M on Black Friday, a busy moviegoing day — but it’s not going to be as busy as last year when all titles minted $75M, boosted by Zootopia 2 and Wicked for Good.

Universal/Paramount’s Focker In-Law was second yesterday with $7.7M at 3,382 theaters, putting its 5-day at $40M for second place.

Disney’s Hexed continues to be cursed with a $4.5M Thanksgiving at 3,725 which was higher than Wish‘s $3.8M Turkey Day but lower than Encanto‘s $5.8M. The Walt Disney Original Animation Title continues to see a $35M 5-day in third place. Disney execs may want to make a trip to the Obsession magic shop today in nearby North Hollywood, buy a Wish Willow and wish for better grosses on Hexed.

Angel Studios’ Hershey officially opened yesterday with a combined day and preview gross of $2.9M at 2,275 theaters, 3-day of $5M and 4-day of $8M in 7th place. The Alexandra Daddario and Finn Wittrock movie is seeing its best grosses in the South with 27% of its gross there. Pic is also playing to norms in East, Midwest, South Central and Mountain. The Penn Cinema in Lititz, PA is Hershey‘s top gross with $31K so far; that a 41-minute drive from Hershey, PA.

Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is losing his mustache with a $590K Thursday, and lower $2.3M 3-day and $3.75M 5-day at 252 theaters in 8th. The David Fincher directed, Quentin Tarantino sequel movie is 79% certified fresh with Rotten Tomatoes critics, down from the 86% of its predecessor, the 2x Oscar winning Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Those who watched the part 2 of the Brad Pitt movie gave it an 88% on RT, which is very good and higher than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood‘s 70% — it’s just not being found in a major way by male dudes. Theater average over 5-days is $14,880 still better than Wake Up Dead Man‘s $7K a year ago.

Neon’s Paper Tiger which is also making a play at specialty house men, but at much lower cost than Cliff Booth, $15M to $200M in production costs, posted a $340K Thanksgiving, on track for a 3-day of $1.65M, 5-day of $3M in its expansion from 28 theaters to 1,332 theaters in 9th place. Neon acquired Paper Tiger before Cannes where the James Gray directed crime noir received a 10 minute standing ovation at its premiere. RT audiences at 66% aren’t far from the pic’s C+ CinemaScore. Not an audience pleaser.

THANKSGIVING AM UPDATE: An alpha female property, Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping with a continued 5-day forecast of $85M+, is stealing business from two other female-leaning movies at the Thanksgiving box office, Universal/Paramount’s Focker In-Law and Disney’s Hexed, both of which are coming in lighter than their forecasts with 5-days of $36M and $35M respectively. That’s essentially a fight for 2nd over the Wednesday-Sunday stretch at this point in time.

Now, that’s not to say that it was silly to date other female pics on top of another tentpole, however, the holiday has shown that two exceptionally pleasing events for the demo can coexist at the same time, read 2024’s Moana 2 and Wicked and even last year’s Wicked: For Good and Zootopia 2. Hexed and Focker In-Law aren’t exceptionally pleasing.

Most movies are expected to ease on average -23% today off their Wednesday daily B.O. as families ease back for festivities. Tomorrow, Black Friday, should see a daily surge between 50%-100% for most titles.

Sunrise on the Reaping‘s $15.1M Wednesday is the second best in the Suzanne Collins’ franchise after 2013’s Catching Fire which did $20.8M on the day before Thanksgiving. 3-day is still on track for $58M+, -51%.

Focker In-Law saw an uptick in its franchise CinemaScore to B+ from previous chapter, 2010’s Little Fockers which received a B-. The original movie 26 years ago has the best grade of A-. The pic is alright with a 64% definite recommend in Screen Engine/Rentrak PostTrak exits. Yesterday was $5.3M with the 3-day at $24.8M. Half of the audience was 18-34 yesterday, 46% over 35 and 64% female overall. Diversity demos were 37% Caucasian, 33% Latino and Hispanic, 13% Black, 10% Asian American and 7% Native American/other. PLFs rep 17% of the gross so far with the John Hamburg directed sequel (the first two pics were helmed by Jay Roach, the third by Paul Weitz) playing best in the West, South, and South Central. AMC Burbank is the top venue with $21k. Again, the Uni and Paramount co-production cost $90M net before global P&A.

Disney’s $200M Hexed is waiting for a box office spell tomorrow that could raise this original animated movie above the doldrums of the studio’s Thanksgiving 2023 dud Wish ($175M production cost, $8.1M Wednesday, $19.6M 3-day, $31.6M 5-day and final domestic of $63.9M). Hexed made $7.6M yesterday (including Tuesday previews) and is eyeing a 3-day of $20M. Hexed gets an A- just like Wish did. PostTrak shows 62% definite recommend for the general audience while kids under 12 gave it a 96% in the top 2 and a 51% must see right away. Kids under 12 rep 31% of the audience while 35-44 (parents) showed up at 31%. Diversity demos were 48% Caucasian, 26% Latino and Hispanic, 9% Black, 7% Asian American and 9% Native American/other.

Again, there are no original songs in this movie about a mother and daughter witch, the latter who realizes her powers as both are transported into another portal where they are trying to save their own kind from doom.

Like Focker-in-Law, Hexed is sharing PLFs with Sunrise on the Reaping which owns most of the holiday supply, those screens are counting 17% of the animated pic’s holiday B.O. so far. 3D is driving 12%. West, South, South Central, Midwest and Mountain are the best markets with the East soft performing 2% below the norm this week. AMC Dine-In Disney Springs Florida is the best location with $52k.

Paramount’s Ebenezer is looking at 4th place at 3,180 theaters with $1.6M yesterday, and still $6.8M-$7.3M third weekend, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s I Play Rocky with $1.4M yesterday at 2,711 sites, $6.6M 3-day, -29%, 5-day of $9.6M and total of $22.6M by EOD Sunday.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 252 locations, boosted by AMC Imax. Wednesday’s opening day estimate was $910K, 3-day is looking at $3.3M and a 5-day of $4.85M. At that level, the theater average over 5-days is $19,2K which is higher than what Netflix pulled did last Thanksgiving with Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery which had a per theater of $7K. Note that Rian Johnson directed thriller was booked in more theaters at 600 sites. Still a bit more robust result here on a limited basis than Wake Up Dead Man ($4.25M 5-day), but alas, Netflix, you’re leaving soooo much money on the table and there’s more than a enough room in this marketplace to have gone wide and minted at least $20M for this sequel to beloved fan Quentin Tarantino pic Once Upon a Time in Hollywood which at $142.8M is the Oscar winning filmmaker’s second highest grossing movie at the domestic B.O. Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher told Collider that the pic cost $120M-$123M, not $200M. We’ll leave it to Wall Street to figure out the downstream.

There’s a shot that Neon’s third weekend wide expansion of James Gray’s crime noir, Paper Tiger, based on the filmmaker’s life, comes in higher than Cliff Booth. Wednesday was an estimated $950K which translates into a $4.4M 3-day, 5-day of $5.1M at 1,322 (+1,294) theaters. Running total by Sunday is around $5.7M. Audiences weren’t wild about the Miles Teller, Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson movie giving it a C+.

Angel Studio’s Hershey biopic about the chocolate maker with Alexandra Daddario and Finn Wittrock got a leg up with early shows yesterday with $1.3M including $534K estimated previews. No firm projection yet, but it was always expected to file in the single digits over its ‘4-day’ start. The pic doesn’t officially open until Thursday and all that preview cash will be rolled into day one. CinemaScore audiences love it with an A, and PostTrak isn’t shabby with 83% positive and a 69% definite recommend, but critics didn’t have a sweet tooth for it 17% Rotten. Male-to-female turnout was 50/50 with the Angel faithful attending at 37% over 55, and 51% over 45. Diversity demos are 61% Caucasian, 17% Black, 13% Latino and Hispanic, 6% Asian American, and 3% Native American/other.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON: If extreme weather doesn’t shutter theaters in the Northeast, then Lionsgate is looking forward to a lucrative Thanksgiving stretch with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping potentially banking $85M+ over five-days.

Should the sixth title in the Suzanne Collins series file in that range, it will rep the second best Thanksgiving haul for a Hunger Games movie after Catching Fire‘s $109.9M Wednesday-Sunday turkey take 13 years ago. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s Wednesday is looking like $15.5M-$16.5M with a second 3-day weekend around $58M-$65M at 4,018 theaters, -46% to -51%. Five day forecasts are always a challenge for the industry to predict: Business dips on Thanksgiving then spikes on Black Friday, which is one of the most active moviegoing days of the year. By Sunday, we’re looking at a running cume for the Francis Lawrence directed movie of $233M domestic, which would be 40% higher than the lifetime cume on 2023’s Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

Second will either be Disney’s Hexed at 3,725 theaters or Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law at 3,382 sites. Hexed is seeing around $7.8M today (including $2.1M previews), for a 3-day around $20M and 5-day between $35M-$40M. Let’s see if this picks up before passing complete judgement on this $200M original animation production, but it’s clear Hexed isn’t Coco or Frozen.

Focker In-Law is seeing a $5.2M Wednesday, 3-day of $24.8M and 5-day of $36.1M. No Rotten Tomatoes audience scores yet on either title.

Fourth goes to Paramount’s third frame of Johnny Depp Christmas movie, Ebenezer with $1.5M today at 3,180 sites and a 3-day between $6.8M-$7.3M, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s fourth frame of I Play Rocky at 2,711 with $1.4M today, 3-day of $6.6M, and 5-day of $9.5M for a running cume of $22.5M.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 251 locations with $1M today, $3M 3-day and 5-day of $5M.

WEDNESDAY AM: As we told you last night, Lionsgate scored its best Tuesday ever at the domestic box office with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and the best ever for the Suzanne Collins franchise as the day raked in $15.98M.

2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire owned the previous best Tuesday for the franchise with $15.96M. Running cume for the fifth Francis Lawrence movie is $148.1M and by Thanksgiving, Sunrise on the Reaping will surpass its previous 2023 chapter’s lifetime domestic B.O. of $166.3M.

As we told you, Sunrise on the Reaping will dominate the Thanksgiving Wednesday through Sunday stretch as the franchise has historically done before since 2013, this time with a floor of $70M+. Previously, the pics over Thanksgiving cooked up the following: Catching Fire ($109.9M), Mockingjay Part 1 ($82.6M), Mockingjay Part 2 ($75.9M) with Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes way behind ($42.2M).

Lionsgate has had back-to-back global hit openings this year with Sunrise on the Reaping last weekend at $226.1M WW and Michael with $218.8M. This has all happened under the administration and watch of Motion Picture Chairman, Adam Fogelson. Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary’s bid.

Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed came in with $2.1M, $100K above the $2M we were spotting yesterday. That preview figure is higher than Encanto ($1.5M previews, 5-day of $40.5M) and Wish ($1.8M previews including $500K Saturday sneaks; 5-day of $31.6M). No RT audience score yet, but critics were meh at 67% fresh. There is a chance that the traditional Disney pic comes in lower than its 5-day forecast of $40M-$45M as original animated titles are very challenging to launch in the streaming era, but you have to start some place.

Universal and Paramount’s Focker In-Law, which didn’t have previews last night, rather began showtimes at midnight, has more potential to hit its 5-day forecast of $45M given the Ariana Grande factor and the fact that audiences love the franchise. The first Meet the Parents 26 years ago was the fave among critics at 85% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Focker-in-Law isn’t the worst at 26%, as that belongs to 2010’s Little Fockers. 2004’s Meet the Fockers stands at 39%.

Hexed, Focker-in-Law and Sunrise on the Reaping are sharing PLFs with the latter having Imax screens (except for AMC where they are being designated to Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth).

Thank God for Lionsgate Hunger Games at the box office: Sans a Wicked, Moana and a Zootopia, the Thanksgiving box office will certainly be down from last year’s five day robust $290.3M, which was the fifth best ever. Moana 2 and Wicked led the holiday to its best haul ever with $424.9M.

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box.
