#3081. How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons

The Europa Clipper will probe below the frozen surface for possible habitats for life

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA's Europa Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's icy moon in the 2030s.

On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper.

Tim Larson Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter?

Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy. It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter.

The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly?

Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys.

We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera.

The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)?

Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible.

How are Europa Clipper’s electronics different from other probes?

Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault—everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts). To get our usual factor-of-two margin, we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads.

That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that.

How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime?

Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3080. DeepSeek pays for outside test of whether V4 Pro could escape human control

Beijing’s Concordia AI found safety gains in the open-weight model, but warned its safeguards can still be bypassed.

DeepSeek has paid an outside firm to test whether its flagship AI model could escape human control, the South China Morning Post reported on Saturday. The evaluation of V4 Pro was carried out by Concordia AI, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy, and published on Wednesday.

Concordia found that the model showed limited ability to copy itself or deceive its creators, according to the SCMP. However, in some tests it resisted attempts to shut it down.

The report covers five risk areas, including cyberattacks, biological and chemical risks, harmful manipulation and loss of human control. It found that the August version of V4 Pro was much safer than the version released in April.

But those gains depend on safeguards that skilled attackers can get around, Concordia warned. That is a particular risk because V4 Pro is open-weight, meaning anyone can download and change it. Most leading Chinese models are released this way.

Other testers have raised similar concerns. In an earlier stress test, US research group FAR.AI said V4 Pro’s built-in safeguards were brittle across high-risk areas.

DeepSeek commissioned the work but agreed not to review, change or block its findings, Concordia told the SCMP. DeepSeek did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.

“The independence of third parties is key in raising trust in evaluation results,” said Cheng Yuan, Concordia’s senior manager for AI safety and governance, according to the SCMP.

DeepSeek is the latest Chinese AI developer to seek outside checks. Earlier this month, Tencent worked with safety firms Alice and Fangcun AI to test its Hy4 model before release.

In the US, a government evaluation by NIST’s AI standards centre found in May that V4 Pro trailed leading US models by about eight months.

#3079. Apple’s new ‘HomeView’ is exactly the home product I’ve been waiting for

Apple has launched several exciting new products in the last month, including iPhone Duo and the redesigned MacBook Pro. But my personal favorite new product is Apple’s HomeView. Here’s how I’ve been using it.

Two years ago when Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on Apple’s forthcoming HomeView, I was immediately ready to buy one.

After numerous delays, the HomeView is finally here. And despite several shortcomings I expect will be fixed with software updates, the HomeView overall is exactly what I’ve been wanting in a home product.

HomeView is essentially a HomePod, but with a screen. And that screen adds so much extra value.

When rumors said the HomeView would only have a 7-inch display, I was concerned it would be too small. It turns out, Apple knew what it was doing. The HomeView’s size is a feature, not a bug. Too much larger and it would stand out as a piece of tech. By staying small, the HomeView can be a cute, non-distracting addition to the home.

Here are some HomeView features I’ve been loving so far:

None of these is what I’d call a “killer feature,” but together they amount to a delightful experience. I already liked having a HomePod around, and HomeView builds on that foundation in so many ways.

Overall, HomeView is very much the product I was hoping for back in 2024. That said, there’s definitely room for improvement. Here’s what’s missing.

I love HomeView for what it is today, but I fully expect Apple to improve the product via software updates. Leaks already point to two major feature upgrades in the works that I hope ship soon.

Built-in apps for Apple Photos and Notes would be great to have, plus support for the recipes included in Apple News+. But my personal top request is for parental controls of some sort.

I completely agree, this is exactly the device I’ve been waiting for.

My only con… Siri AI is just slightly more than half-baked when it comes to voice prompts. One example, when we ask it for the weather forecast it gives us a one-line “It’s going to rain today.” That’s not a forecast. 🙃 So we’re forced to follow up with “more details please”. When we do… 🙂 … we get an actual forecast. Asking it for a recap of today’s headlines is hit or miss too. These are just two of a handful of examples where Siri AI is only about 60% of what Alexa+ is for conversational AI purposes.

With that one nod to the nut jobs out there claiming an old iPad suffices everyone on planet earth perfectly well, I’m still giddy about the fact that I can browse through my full library of music on Apple Music, Amazon Music, and iBroadcast and try new “suggested” albums/playlists without having to have my iPhone with me everywhere I go in the house. While I spent $299 mainly for an enhanced music experience, having it is priceless.

For a device that’s intended for the whole family, I’ve been surprised to find there are no current features to prevent young children from doing whatever they want with HomeView. I have a toddler who loves the HomeView so much that I had to move it out of his reach. I wish there was a way to lock the screen on command, or prevent switching apps or faces without authentication. Some sort of “toddler mode” would be greatly appreciated.

Siri AI has also had some bugs, but those are likely related to me running the iOS 27.3 beta.

Apple’s new HomeView is available now for $299.

What’s your take on the HomeView so far? Are you still mulling a purchase? Let us know in the comments.

#3077. We May Be Witnessing Wall Street's 2 Biggest Bubbles Bursting Simultaneously

The stock market’s No. 1 catalyst and its $1.5 trillion risk-measuring powder keg appear ready to pop.

By Sean Williams – Nov 28, 2026 at 9:06AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Since October 2022, it's been all systems go for what's arguably the greatest wealth creator on the planet. The ageless Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +1.18%) bounced as much as 90% off its 2022 bear market low, while the benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) and growth-stock-dominated Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.31%) more than doubled in value.

Several factors have lit a fire under Wall Street's four-year (and counting) bull market rally, including record S&P 500 share buybacks, better-than-expected corporate earnings, excitement for brand-name stock splits, and initial public offering euphoria. But nothing has been more important than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and the ongoing AI data center build-out.

AI is Wall Street's biggest technological leap forward since the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s. Unfortunately, parabolic moves higher in the stock market often have consequences.

Although history has conclusively shown that the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite climb over multiple decades, historical precedent isn't as kind to investors over shorter time frames. Eventually, something always pushes equities over the edge, and we may be witnessing the simultaneous bursting of Wall Street's two biggest bubbles right now.

While past events can never guarantee directional moves for the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite, history has a way of rhyming on Wall Street more often than not. One indicator that has an immaculate track record of foreshadowing what's to come is outstanding margin debt.

Margin is money an investor borrows from their broker, with interest, to short-sell (wager against) or purchase securities. When margin is used to buy stocks or exchange-traded funds, it represents a form of leverage.

Using margin for purchases can be especially risky. Margin can magnify an investor's gains if a security moves in the desired direction, but can quickly amplify losses if it moves in the opposite direction. This dynamic makes investors' use of margin a crude but particularly useful measure of their willingness to take risks.

Total Margin Debt hits $1.5 Trillion, a new all-time high 🤯 👀 pic.twitter.com/1IXqZGgrqs

While outstanding margin debt at brokers, as reported monthly by FINRA, is expected to climb in lockstep with the stock market over time, trouble arises when it goes parabolic over a relatively short time frame (12 to 19 months). There have been four instances since 1998 when margin debt has skyrocketed by at least 65% over a short period, and the prior three occurrences were all precursors to disaster on Wall Street:

Since June, margin debt has tapered to $1.448 trillion as of October. While this drop doesn't guarantee that Wall Street's $1.5 trillion risk-taking bubble has officially burst, historical precedent certainly suggests it has.

In addition to Wall Street's $1.5 trillion margin powder keg potentially going "boom," the AI bubble also appears to be bursting.

Let me preface this discussion by stating that AI remains a bona fide long-term growth driver. This technology offers genuine productivity and efficiency improvements across most sectors and industries around the globe. The question isn't whether AI is viable -- it's how long it takes for businesses to optimize this technology.

Since the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s, every game-changing technology has navigated an early-innings bubble-bursting event. This includes the internet, genome decoding, nanotechnology, 3D printing, blockchain technology, and the metaverse, to name some of the more prominent tech-driven innovations.

The reason these bubbles repeatedly form and subsequently burst is that investors constantly overestimate the pace of adoption and/or optimization of new technologies.

Both 3D printing and the metaverse had clear adoption issues, with the initial hype never translating into widespread adoption. But this isn't the case for AI, which has seen neoclouds and hyperscalers spend small fortunes to expand their AI data centers.

Stock market bubbles throughout history…AI stocks now ~40% of the market. pic.twitter.com/RxSAh09k6F

The issue for the AI revolution is that businesses aren't particularly close to optimizing AI solutions. It took until several years after the dot-com bubble burst for internet-driven companies to optimize these solutions to boost sales and profits. AI companies are likely on the same trajectory.

The bond market is also signaling a potential bursting of the AI bubble.

When public companies issue debt, it's priced at par value. Bond prices should remain around par value if traders are confident in the underlying company's ability to service and repay its debt.

But throughout much of 2026, bond prices for foundational AI companies have plunged, while corresponding yields have soared. This disconnect suggests that the bond market is growing increasingly skeptical about the sustainability of the AI infrastructure build-out and/or of AI companies' ability to meet their debt obligations.

For all intents and purposes, we may be witnessing Wall Street's two biggest bubbles bursting at the same time.

#3076. This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer

Dinesh Rai’s role as Boston Children’s prompt engineer quickly outgrew its bounds

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist.

In his home office, Dinesh Rai splits his time between working with engineers and clinicians at Boston Children’s Hospital.

When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.

At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.

Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.

Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.

When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.

Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”

For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.

Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.

For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.

His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.

That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.

At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.

One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.

The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.

Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.

Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.

Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.

Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.

Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.

“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”

In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?

That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.

Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”

The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.

What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.

That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.

“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist focusing on technology.

#3073. Why Abercrombie & Fitch Stock Surged This Week

Investors need the sales momentum to continue with Abercrombie stock trading at a 52-week high.

By Howard Smith – Nov 28, 2026 at 9:06AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Abercrombie & Fitch ›

A blowout third-quarter earnings beat and raised full-year outlook sent Abercrombie & Fitch (ANF +4.22%) soaring 33.7% this week.

Abercrombie & Fitch stock changed hands at $184.43 as of the close on Friday, Nov. 27, up 33.7% this week from last Friday's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) was up 5.6%, and the Nasdaq-100 was up 6.78%.

Management reported third-quarter net sales of $1.44 billion on Tuesday, an 11% increase year over year that beat Wall Street consensus estimates of $1.37 billion. Adjusted earnings per share reached $3.82, handily topping the $3.08 expected by analysts, while operating margin expanded to 15.5%. Profitability was aided by a $20 million pre-tax tariff refund, which reduced costs by $0.40 per share. "The strong top line, coupled with disciplined inventory management, enabled us to deliver healthy sales growth with higher AUR [average unit retail] and lower promotions," CEO Fran Horowitz said.

Abercrombie & Fitch sells casual apparel and accessories through its namesake and Hollister brands to teens and young adult consumers. Both major brand families contributed to the quarterly surge, with Abercrombie sales climbing 12% to $688.8 million and Hollister sales growing 11% to $746.6 million. Tight inventory control across the retail footprint reduced the need for clearance discounts, enabling the business to capture full-price sales in both domestic and international markets.

Following the third-quarter performance, management raised its full-year fiscal 2026 net sales growth target to around 6% and lifted diluted earnings per share guidance to a range of $13.70 to $13.90. The retailer also reiterated its commitment to repurchase at least $500 million of its own shares this year. This week's guidance raise confirms that Abercrombie's inventory discipline and pricing power are holding up despite broader apparel headwinds.

Investors now turn their attention to the crucial holiday shopping period. For the fourth quarter, management expects net sales growth of roughly 7% and earnings per share between $4.40 and $4.60, which sits slightly below the $4.84 consensus estimate. The company expects to report full-year fiscal 2026 earnings on March 3, 2027.

From a valuation perspective, Abercrombie & Fitch trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 14. The stock sits at its 52-week high (as of its close on Nov. 27, 2026), meaning the market has priced in high expectations for continued operational execution.

Retail and apparel consumers can be picky, with trends coming and going. Abercrombie & Fitch's core brands are clearly consumer favorites right now, with multi-year sales growth. Trading at a 52-week high, though, suggests investors expect that momentum to continue.

The risks are real, too, and need to be considered. Guidance earlier this year assumed 15% global tariffs and flagged a strategic geographic review. Q3 profit also included a $20 million operating income benefit from tariff refunds, which is one-time and flatters results. Middle East conflict impacted demand, especially at Hollister.

Inventory rose to $763 million from $601 million at fiscal year-end, a level that could force markdowns if demand cools. Fashion cycles can also fade fast. But Abercrombie has generated significant cash from operations this year, proving it is managing the business well.

Investors could do well buying the stock here, but should remember that the stock price already reflects the current success. Any stumbles ahead could hit the stock, so investors should consider that risk when allocating funds.

#3072. macOS 27.3 adds three new Mac features, here’s what’s coming

macOS 27.3 is launching next month alongside iOS 27.3 and more, and it includes a variety of new features for Mac users. Here are three macOS 27.3 features coming soon.

macOS already supports running Live Activities from your iPhone via iPhone Mirroring. But in macOS 27.3, Apple is adding native support for Live Activities from Mac apps.

The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the new Dynamic Island. But with macOS 27.3, the new feature expands to all Mac models and in a slightly different way.

Live Activities on Macs without a Dynamic Island will display in the menu bar. From there you can click to view full details, as seen above.

Safari introduces several upgrades across macOS 27.3, iOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3.

Vertical Tabs are one tentpole addition, providing a new option for how to view your tabs in Apple’s browser. When enabled, your tabs move from the top of the browser to the left side in a new column view.

Adaptive Dark Mode is another new feature. It automatically enables dark mode on many websites that don’t natively support it already. Finally, Siri AI gains support for new Safari actions, including the ability to interact with a full webpage using onscreen awareness, not just the parts that are currently visible.

Do you use Markdown, the popular John Gruber-created plain text syntax? If so, macOS 27.3 has a welcome addition: support for rendering Markdown in Quick Look.

Rather than needing to open Markdown files in apps to preview formatted text, macOS now lets you just use Quick Look and see all of your Markdown syntax rendered properly with links, headings, bold, italics, and more.

You can learn more about Markdown here on John Gruber’s site, Daring Fireball.

Which macOS 27.3 additions are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3071. Morningstar vs. Toast: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Morningstar's steady data business faces off against Toast's fast-growing restaurant software, and the valuation gap may tilt the decision.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 28, 2026 at 9:12AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Morningstar ›

Choosing between a steady data provider and a high-growth software platform can be a difficult task for investors. Many are currently weighing the established presence of Morningstar (MORN -2.01%) against the rapid expansion of Toast (TOST +2.85%).

Morningstar provides essential research and analytics to investors and financial firms, while Toast offers a comprehensive operating system for the restaurant industry. Although they serve different markets, both companies leverage deep data and integrated technology platforms to build long-term relationships. They represent two different paths to potential growth for your portfolio.

Morningstar offers independent investment insights and data to a wide range of clients, including advisors and asset managers. The company distributes its research through platforms such as Morningstar Direct and PitchBook, while forming key technology alliances with firms such as Microsoft Corp.(MSFT +0.60%). This diverse customer base helps the firm maintain its position as a central player in the global financial ecosystem.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $2.6 billion, representing growth of approximately 9.4%. The company reported net income of around $445.5 million during this same period. This performance shows a steady upward revenue trajectory compared with previous years, illustrating the consistent demand for financial data.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 1.2x, indicating that its total debt is slightly higher than its shareholders' equity. The current ratio, a measure of the company's ability to cover its short-term obligations, was approximately 1.0x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, the firm generated free cash flow of roughly $442.6 million, representing the cash remaining after paying for operations and capital equipment.

Toast provides an integrated platform that includes software, hardware, and payment processing services designed specifically for the restaurant industry. The company primarily serves small- and medium-sized businesses but is actively expanding into larger enterprise accounts, such as Ruby Tuesday. This focus on tech stocks and the dining sector allows the company to provide tailored tools for point-of-sale and kitchen management.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $7.2 billion, which was an increase of approximately 22%. Net income for the period was around $550 million, marking a significant transition into profitability compared to earlier years. This rapid top-line expansion illustrates the company's ability to capture market share within its specialized niche.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the firm reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x and a current ratio of roughly 2.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $608.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) accounted for roughly 36.6% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Morningstar faces potential reputational damage if its independence or conflicts of interest are called into question, especially in its credit ratings and advisory segments. The firm competes with major providers like S&P Global (SPGI +0.11%) and must navigate the high costs associated with innovating in the artificial intelligence space. Additionally, its revenue is sensitive to the cyclical nature of financial markets and shifting global regulations.

Toast is currently managing a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission regarding how it applies consumer protection laws to its business contracts. The company also operates in a highly competitive market and must maintain system reliability as it scales its infrastructure. Furthermore, as a payment facilitator, the business is deeply dependent on third-party bank partners and remains susceptible to fluctuations in consumer spending.

Toast carries a lower P/S ratio, which measures market capitalization divided by sales over the past twelve months, while Morningstar offers a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Toast continues to add thousands of restaurants each quarter as that industry seeks a single platform to handle a myriad of tasks, like employee scheduling, point-of-sale transactions, tip automation, back-office needs, loyalty programs, handling takeout orders, and personalized marketing to customers.

All that should bring in 2027 revenue of $8.89 billion, which would be a rise of about 19% from 2026's expected full-year sales of $7.49 billion. Net income next year should touch $732 million, up about $140 million from 2026.

Longer term, Toast management sees opportunities to expand into gas station convenience stores, since most are small businesses, and into sports and entertainment facilities, which do a high volume of business per event.

Morningstar, meanwhile, offers investors steadily compounding returns over time, combining a long track record of dividend growth with a diversified business model built on subscriptions, institutional data feeds, and wealth management software. Because its offerings focus on information and software rather than lending, the company faces less direct credit risk than traditional banks, while still offering a modest dividend that increased 10% a year ago to $0.50 per share quarterly.

Over the past year, Morningstar's stock has gained more than 10%, fueled in part by an October rally tied to strong financial and AI-related momentum. Alongside reporting growing AI adoption across several products and solid third-quarter gains in revenue, operating income, and profit margins on Oct. 28, the company benefited early in the month from OpenAI's launch of ChatGPT for Financial Services, which integrates private market data from Morningstar's PitchBook unit.

Top-line growth is good, not great. For 2026, sales will rise about 9% to $2.67 billion, with 2027 expected to bring a 6% gain to $2.83 billion, with net income of $443 million, a much healthier 18% gain from 2026.

Which stock is the better buy? Morningstar is appealing for the long-term positive effect of dividends on a portfolio, but Toast's ability to consolidate functions in the highly fragmented restaurant industry promises excellent growth for years to come. Even as it comes at a slight premium to the typical S&P 500 stock, on a forward P/E basis, Toast is worth paying up for.

#3070. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

#3069. iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m currently using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer …

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

What I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

The size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

My preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen

While the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I said when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

It’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an issue at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI ).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

The aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the new Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

The Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The issue is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

The rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the issue, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

One of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller issue than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

I said in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

I’m where you are. I received mine on Tuesday. It’s too heavy. It’s too expensive, especially with a subpar camera. Touch ID is annoying. The larger screen is going to be rarely used in my day-to-day. Giving up the larger main screen for a screen I’ll rarely use for an extra $1000 seems kinda dumb.

But every so often I open an app or webpage on the larger screen and it’s pretty amazing.

I’ll probably return it. But my choice isn’t the duo or the 18 Pro. By doing away with the iPhone upgrade program and not releasing a pro phone with groundbreaking advancements Apple has removed my incentive to move to the 18. If I send the Duo back I’ll keep my 17 Pro, and see what the Air 2 offers. Much like I moved from the larger, heavier MBP to the smaller, lighter MBA when its power far surpassed what I need I may do the same with my phone if the next gen of the iPhone Air is compelling enough.

My head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

In previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

Apple recently launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but three more new iPhone models will reportedly arrive in early 2027. Here’s what’s coming.

iPhone 18 was conspicuously absent from Apple’s annual September event this year. Instead, the company launched iPhone 18 Pro and kept iPhone 17 around as the base model.

But the iPhone 18 is still coming, expected to launch in early 2027—likely February or March.

The basic design of the iPhone 18 is expected to stay unchanged as Apple prioritizes internal upgrades. Rumored new features include a more powerful A20 chip with at least a slight RAM bump, plus increased battery life.

We’re not expecting iPhone 18 Pro’s camera upgrades, smaller Dynamic Island, or vapor chamber to come to the base model. One question mark is the C2 cellular modem. iPhone 17 uses a Qualcomm modem, and it’s unclear whether that will be the case with iPhone 18 as well.

Apple also has a lower-cost iPhone 18e model reportedly in the works. It’s expected to launch around the same time as iPhone 18.

Reporting indicates the iPhone 18 and 18e might be more similar than prior corresponding models. Improvements coming to the 18e include:

ProMotion is expected to be missing from the new model, which will still have a 60Hz display. And while big rear camera upgrades are unlikely, a recent CAD leak suggests iPhone 18e might get a larger camera bump.

The iPhone Air 2 will reportedly aim to address two of the top wishes users had for the first-gen model. Those two upgrades are:

By adding a second rear camera, iPhone Air 2 will at least offer camera parity with the base iPhone—something the original Air couldn’t with its single camera.

Battery life gains could ease concerns about the iPhone Air 2 running a full day on a charge. And hopefully the Air 2 will benefit from positive word-of-mouth about the first model.

Another tentpole addition is the A20 Pro chip, which might include one less GPU core than iPhone 18 Pro but otherwise be very similar.

Following the introduction of these three iPhone models in early 2027, Apple is expected to launch new Pro and Duo models in fall 2027.

#3066. I’ve tested Ubuntu 27.04 ahead of its April release – and it will wow you

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

One thing that surprised me is that Myna (Ubuntu’s AI dictation tool) has yet to find its way into the Ubuntu ISO as a default app. As with Ubuntu 26.10, you can install it, but you have to first add the necessary repository with:

With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

#3065. The 3 Best Places to Stash Your Retirement Savings in 2027

Where you put your retirement savings is almost as important as how much you save.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 28, 2026 at 9:15AM EST

You might have a goal for how much you want to save toward your retirement each month in 2027. That's a great start, but it's only one of the critical decisions you'll have to make if you hope to increase your retirement readiness next year.

You'll also have to decide where you want to keep those funds so they can do you the most good. Here are three of the best options worth considering, along with the pros and cons of each.

A 401(k) is your best place to begin if you qualify for a match from your employer. This is essentially a bonus that you'll only get if you save money in your 401(k). If you don't, you'll miss out on thousands of dollars in additional retirement savings.

After you've claimed your 401(k) match, you can continue saving here if you like your investment options. 401(k)s enable adults under 50 to save up to $25,500 in 2027, with older adults able to save even more, so it's a great choice for those who want to set aside a lot of money for retirement next year. However, investment options are usually more limited than what you'd find with an IRA.

IRAs give you much greater flexibility over your investments. You can choose to invest in just about anything you'd like and change them up as often as you want. You can also choose when you want to pay taxes on your funds.

You fill traditional IRAs with pre-tax dollars and Roth IRAs with after-tax dollars. In retirement, you owe taxes on your traditional IRA withdrawals, but not your Roth IRA withdrawals.

The downside to IRAs is that contribution limits are much lower. They're remaining at $7,500 for adults under 50 in 2027, with adults 50 and over able to save up to $8,600 next year. High earners who wish to contribute to Roth IRAs may have lower limits.

Health savings accounts (HSAs) are technically designed to hold medical savings, but they operate much like IRAs, with the added benefit of tax-free medical withdrawals at any age. But you can only open one of these if you have an individual health insurance plan with a deductible of $1,750 or more or a family plan with a deductible of $3,500 or more in 2027.

If you meet these criteria, you can contribute up to $4,500 to an HSA next year if you have a qualifying individual health insurance plan, or up to $9,000 with a qualifying family plan. Adults 55 and older can add another $1,000 to these limits.

It's also fine to use more than one retirement account if you'd like. For example, you can start with your 401(k) until you've claimed your entire match. Then, switch to your IRA, and if you max that out, move on to your HSA. Think about what works best for you and have a plan for where those first dollars will go when 2027 arrives.

It's the closest thing to my mirrorless camera

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In my ongoing quest to test the best camera phones around, I’ve been immersing myself in phones from the other side of the world. It all started with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max a couple of months back and then the RedMagic 11S Pro recently, but now I find myself at yet another crossroads with the Vivo X500 Pro Max.

I’ve been using it for over three weeks now, and all I can say about it so far is that it’s an impressive piece of gear, especially when paired with its new 400mm Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra lens. While my iPhone 18 Pro Max has set the gold standard for consistent, reliable photos and video, the Vivo X500 Pro Max has officially dethroned it as my daily camera. Here’s why.

The Vivo X500 Pro Max is easily one of the most capable camera phones I've tested, pairing a 50MP main sensor with a massive 200MP ZEISS periscope telephoto lens that doubles as a telemacro shooter. It also packs a 7,800mAh battery, 6.85-inch 144Hz AMOLED display, and there's an optional telephoto converter kit that increases the range of its telephoto camera.

Let me start off by explaining the camera specs of both phones. Usually, I don’t lean heavily on specs, but Vivo X500 Pro Max vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max deserves a deeper dive.

For years, I haven't really cared much about the iPhone’s camera specs because its performance speaks for itself — and the 18 Pro Max doesn’t disappoint. It’s notable for its triple 48MP camera system, highlighted by a new four-step variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0) on the main lens, giving shooters physical control over how much light hits the sensor and, inevitably, the depth of field.

That main sensor is paired with a 48MP ultrawide and a 48MP telephoto with 4x optical zoom, plus an 18MP Center Stage front camera. On the video side, it’s a beast and gets a boost from the addition of Pro Controls, offering up to 4K 120fps native recording and cinema-grade tools including ProRes RAW, Apple Log 2, and Genlock support.

Meanwhile, the Vivo X500 Pro Max counters with a powerful triple-camera system headlined by a 50MP main camera with up to 17 stops of dynamic range, paired with a 50MP ultrawide. The most impressive piece is the massive 200MP telephoto shooter with 3.5x optical zoom that is also capable of telemacro shots.

What makes it feel more like a bridge camera is how it can be paired with optional 200mm and 400mm external ZEISS telephoto extenders. They effectively increase the range of the telephoto camera, putting the iPhone to shame. Rounding out the hardware is a 50MP autofocus selfie camera. When it comes to video, it’s capable of 8K recording, native 4K 240fps slow-motion, and 4K 120fps 10-bit 4:2:2 Log recording.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In the side-by-side comparison shots I captured throughout New York City above, one trend quickly stood out: the Vivo X500 Pro Max has a penchant for producing a brighter image — and it comes at a cost.

In high-contrast scenes, that extra brightness does a great job of lifting shadows and pulling out fine details that the iPhone 18 Pro Max leaves in the dark. However, that aggressive exposure often pushes bright areas too far and leaves highlights overblown. By comparison, the iPhone manages to keep them controlled.

That same pattern carries over into low-light shooting with the main camera, where the Vivo consistently delivers a brighter overall shot.

If there is one area where the Vivo X500 Pro Max leaves the iPhone 18 Pro Max in the dust, it’s zoom photography. In every single telephoto shot I captured — like the one by MSG where I pointed the cameras toward a giant advertisement on the side of a building — the Vivo pulled in substantially more detail and crisp definition. Not only does it render individual bricks and distant textures better, but it also delivers a brighter overall tone.

What makes that lens even more impressive is that it pulls double duty as a telemacro shooter. Rather than locking me into the ultrawide lens for close-ups, the telephoto lets me get remarkably close to subjects while still maintaining sharp clarity. Just look at the progressive shots of the parakeet as I got closer — I really love the crisp details of its feathers.

The biggest compliment I can give the Vivo X500 Pro Max is that it makes me genuinely consider leaving my dedicated mirrorless camera behind. Once I attach the optional 400mm telephoto conversion lens, the phone stops behaving like a smartphone and starts delivering authentic optical zoom.

Instead of relying on artificial portrait-mode blur or heavy digital cropping, the glass produces naturally creamy, out-of-focus backgrounds while keeping subjects in tack-sharp focus — giving photos a true DSLR-style depth that the iPhone 18 Pro Max simply can’t replicate.

Just look at the street photography snapshots I captured above, which highlight the optical quality of a combo like this. From the streets of New York, to capturing planes flying overhead, and even a shot of the Great Orion Nebula at night, the telephoto performance is on another level.

After spending more than three weeks with the Vivo X500 Pro Max, I can say it’s officially earned the title of my favorite camera phone. Between its unmatched zoom detail, telemacro versatility, and the mirrorless-like bokeh you get from the 400mm telephoto converter, it’s the first smartphone that has genuinely made me leave my mirrorless camera behind when I commute to work.

That said, all that optical power is a tough pill to swallow because importing the phone alone runs $1,609.99, and tacking on the optional telephoto converter pushes the total well over $2,000. It’s difficult to pull the trigger at that premium, especially when the iPhone 18 Pro Max exists at a much lower price. Still, I can’t overlook the utility that the Vivo X500 Pro Max brings to the table. Combined with the optional telephoto converter lens, it’s a combo I think enthusiasts will certainly appreciate.

#3062. Your Wear OS smartwatch just got a new way to save battery life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It could make your Pixel Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch more power efficient.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s new model worth it?

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future

The update improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch users can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

#3061. Review: Aqara W200 supports Adaptive Temperature in HomeKit at a great price

Earlier this year, my wife and I bought our first house. Along with all the other exciting things, it’s also let me spend a lot of time testing new smart home gear.

One of the most important and useful smart home accessories is a smart thermostat. Six months ago, I installed the Aqara Smart Thermostat W200, and it’s been a fantastic addition to our smart home setup … especially because it supports Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature. Here’s how it works.

Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward. I’d previously installed various Ecobee thermostats. The trickiest part this time was learning the intricacies of the new house itself, which the Aqara app did a good job of guiding me through.

I used the Aqara app for the installation and setup, like choosing an interface design for the thermostat’s display itself. But after that, I closed the app and haven’t opened it since. Everything now is managed through the Apple Home app, and I appreciate that the Aqara app lets me do this without any pushback. It doesn’t try to pull me back into it to sell me a subscription or show me ads.

This matters because the Aqara app is nothing to write home about. It has a lot of settings, but I don’t think it’s particularly elegant or user-friendly. You can choose from a small collection of different screensavers. The thermostat’s interface is similar to the app in that it’s very utilitarian, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing for quick manual temperature adjustments.

The Aqara W200 also has a mmWave radar sensor that detects your presence. When you walk up to it, that sensor detects your approach and the screensaver automatically goes away to reveal the controls. It’s also exposed to HomeKit and can trigger automations. Unfortunately, this isn’t particularly useful for me because of the thermostat’s awkward location.

The Aqara W200’s build quality is good enough. It’s primarily made of plastic, unlike higher-end smart thermostats that feature metal housing, so it doesn’t look super premium on your wall. It has a responsive 4-inch touchscreen. It has a small footprint overall, so you’ll likely need the included back trim plate if your previous thermostat required a larger opening in the wall.

The standout feature of the Aqara W200, though, is its support for Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature, which debuted as part of iOS 26. As of right now, the Aqara W200 is the only thermostat with Adaptive Temperature support available, though two more are coming next year as part of Apple’s new Home Collection suite.

Adaptive Temperature is Apple’s feature that will automatically adjust your thermostat’s temperature based on your preferences. It uses your location and the location of other home members to determine when to adjust the thermostat.

Once you enable Adaptive Temperature, you set your ideal temperature range for the following states:

My wife and I set our preferred temperature ranges for each scenario. I particularly appreciate the ability to set a different range for night, since we like it noticeably colder overnight than during the day.

After that setup process, Adaptive Temperature has worked in the background without any involvement from us. It passively uses all the information on our iPhones to make its decision.

“Your iPhone uses on-device intelligence to predict when you’re on your way home to bring it to the correct temperature by the time you get there, and adjusts the thermostat to save energy when you are far away from home,” Apple explains.

Adaptive Temperature uses your iPhone and other home members’ devices to determine when to adjust the temperature. “Home can learn daily routines to predict when you’re likely to arrive and adjust the temperature for you,” Apple says. This includes things like your calendar events.

I can count on one hand the number of times we’ve had to manually adjust the thermostat since installing the W200, and most of those times were because we had guests with different preferences than ours.

Honestly, I thought I wrote this post months ago, but I guess it slipped my mind. I actually think there’s a pretty simple explanation for that, though. I installed the W200, enabled Adaptive Temperature in the Apple Home app, and haven’t thought about it since.

I think that’s a great endorsement of the Aqara W200 as a product. When I build a smart home, I want accessories that I can install, benefit from the “smarts” of, and never have to think about. That’s why I’ve also come to appreciate Lutron, which I’ve installed throughout my entire house. The Aqara W200 falls into that same bucket.

Between the Smart Thermostat W200 and UWB Smart Lock U400 (full review), Aqara powers two key pillars of my smart home, and I’ve been incredibly impressed with both.

The Aqara Smart Thermostat W200 is also very reasonably priced. It retails for $159.99, but is currently on sale for $119.99.

Do you use a HomeKit thermostat in your house? If so, which one? What are your favorite smart home accessories? Let us know down in the comments.

#3060. Prediction: Palantir and Nvidia Will Be Worth This Much by Year-end 2027 (Hint: Only 1 Is a Buy)

Investors looking to choose one of these AI stalwarts for their portfolios have an easy choice to make right now.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 28, 2026 at 9:24AM EST

Palantir Technologies (PLTR +5.25%) and Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) are among the leading players in their respective artificial intelligence (AI) niches. However, shares of both companies have underperformed the technology sector this year.

Palantir stock has lost 3% of its value in 2026, as of this writing, while Nvidia's shares have dropped nearly 21% this year. The Nasdaq-100 Technology Sector index, meanwhile, is up 9% in 2026 despite a significant pullback lately. I will take a closer look at the prospects of both companies in this article and check which AI stock could stage a recovery by the end of 2027.

Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) has been a huge hit among customers, allowing them to integrate generative AI into their business operations to improve decision-making, automate workflows, and reduce redundancy. The productivity improvements delivered by AIP explain why Palantir's growth has accelerated.

The company released its third-quarter results earlier this month, reporting a 96% year-over-year increase in revenue to $2.31 billion. This was the first time Palantir's quarterly revenue surpassed $2 billion. What's more, Palantir's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased to $0.44 last quarter from $0.21 in the year-ago period.

Palantir's stronger earnings growth was driven by increased business from existing customers. The company reported a net dollar retention rate of 165% last quarter. The metric compares the trailing-twelve-month (TTM) revenue from customers in a quarter to the TTM revenue from those same customers in the year-ago period. So, a reading above 100% suggests that Palantir customers have increased adoption of its AI software solutions.

Also, Palantir booked new contracts worth $2.92 billion last quarter, which was higher than its top line. This explains why the company's revenue pipeline improved in Q3, with total remaining deal value (RDV) increasing by 55% year over year to $13.4 billion. The metric represents the total value of contracts that Palantir has yet to fulfill at the end of the quarter, so robust growth in this metric suggests stronger financial performance in the future.

Not surprisingly, Palantir increased its full-year guidance and now expects $8.53 billion in revenue for 2026, representing a 90% increase over last year. Analysts expect Palantir's EPS to jump by 127% this year to $1.70, followed by a 49% increase in 2027, though it can outperform expectations given its ability to extract more business from existing customers.

Nvidia, on the other hand, has been in the news for the wrong reasons lately. However, there is no denying that the company continues to grow at a robust pace due to its solid position in AI chips. Nvidia's revenue in the most recent quarter increased by 103% year over year to $115.8 billion. That was slightly higher than Palantir's growth.

What's more, Nvidia's adjusted EPS grew by 111% year over year to $2.68, slightly higher than Palantir's growth. Nvidia is on track to end fiscal 2027 with almost $424 billion in revenue, which would be a 96% improvement over the prior year. Analysts expect its EPS to increase by 103% in fiscal 2027 to $9.67, followed by another strong 72% increase next year.

So, Nvidia's EPS is anticipated to increase at a significantly faster pace than Palantir. Additionally, a closer look at the valuations of both companies clearly indicates that Nvidia has the potential to deliver bigger gains by the end of 2027.

Nvidia stock is significantly cheaper than Palantir, based on both the earnings and sales multiples. This is evident from the following chart.

Additionally, it is clear that Nvidia's growth is superior to Palantir's, and the hardware specialist could outperform Palantir in 2027, based on Wall Street estimates. It is worth noting that Nvidia has increased its fiscal 2028 revenue growth guidance to 75%, up by five percentage points. Palantir hasn't issued guidance for next year yet, but a significant slowdown in total contract value (TCV) growth to 6% year-over-year in Q3 was alarming.

A slowdown in TCV growth suggests Palantir may be struggling to replenish its revenue pipeline, which could weigh on its growth next year. That's probably why analysts expect slower EPS growth in 2027 than at Nvidia.

Palantir's 2027 EPS is expected to land at $2.54, while Nvidia is projected to report $16.61 in EPS. Given that both companies operate in the tech space, I would use the tech-focused Nasdaq-100 index to gauge where they will be in a year.

The Nasdaq-100 index has a forward earnings multiple of 20. As both Nvidia and Palantir are poised to grow at healthy rates next year, I would put a premium on their valuations. Assuming both companies trade at 25 times earnings at the end of 2027 and Nvidia's EPS jumps to $16.61, its stock price could reach $415.

That's 177% higher than its current stock price. A similar multiple for Palantir would send its stock price to $42 after a year, implying a big slide from current levels. In simpler words, Palantir needs to trade at a significant premium to Nvidia to soar higher over the coming year. This is why I think Nvidia remains the better buy right now, as a combination of solid growth and cheap valuation can set it up for a stronger stock price jump by the end of 2027.
